On Gerhard Nebel, Plato and the Polis—which stands far above Werner Jaeger’s Paideia:
He calls the polis a state. But the state is an even more unique, concrete, historically limited form.

Indeed, it is more so precisely because its form has been sharpened by historical and dialectical development. It belongs to the period from the sixteenth to the twentieth century of the Christian age and is tied to those four centuries. It therefore makes no sense to speak of a medieval “state.”

The state emerged from the Renaissance, Humanism, the Reformation, and the Counter-Reformation. It is the neutralization of religious civil war. It is therefore a very specific achievement of Western rationalism.
To call the polis a state is like going in the other direction and calling belief in Zeus and the other gods a “state religion.”
The state is essentially the product of religious civil war.
More precisely, it comes from the overcoming of that civil war through the neutralization and secularization of the confessional battle lines. That means de-theologization.
The state creates the opposition between inward and outward. It creates the separation between internal and external.
All of this is essential to the state and completely alien to the polis.
